cards.title: Cohort Table Mechanics: Reading Repeat Orders Diagonally
cards.summary: How to build and read a customer cohort table so repeat revenue and lifetime order counts are calculated correctly.
cards.use_when: Building or auditing a monthly cohort report to decide whether repeat-purchase revenue justifies acquisition spend.
steps: Lay out a grid: one row per acquisition month, one column per subsequent month of customer lifetime (month 0, month 1, month 2...).

Row totals give new customer orders in that month; the diagonal is what produces recurring orders in a given month. For June: take May's second month, April's third month, March's fourth month and sum them.
Verify the diagonal sum ties to the returning-customer orders figure reported for that month (in the source example, three diagonal cells summed to 122 recurring orders).

Read the average orders-per-customer by lifetime length: the source cohort showed roughly 1.2 orders in the first month rising to nearly double within six months, and cumulative orders of 1.67 by five months, 1.63 by four.

Use the cohort with the longest history to set your lifetime-orders assumption; the presenter used 1.98 orders for a cohort with the most historical data, explicitly choosing conservatism over extrapolating month 7-9 growth.
Recompute the table every month; if early cohorts' later months keep rising, your lifetime-orders estimate is stale.
caveats: Cohort-derived lifetime orders are only reliable for cohorts old enough to have lived through the period you're measuring; newer cohorts will understate repeat behavior.
The 1.98 figure is a source-specific example, not a benchmark for your store.
Do not read across rows instead of diagonally; that misstates which cohort produced a given month's repeat orders.

cards.title: From First-Order Economics to Lifetime Value
cards.summary: Step-by-step build of first-order contribution margin, LTV, and the CM:CAC ratio so you can see whether acquisition pays back.
cards.use_when: Evaluating whether current ad spend is profitable on a first-order and lifetime basis before scaling acquisition.
steps: Compute first-order revenue as AOV times one order; in the source example AOV $138 produced $138 revenue, and subtracting product and fulfillment cost left $100 contribution margin.
Divide contribution margin by CAC for the first-order ratio; at $100 CM versus $97 CAC the ratio was 1.02, i.e. about $2 of profit on the first order.
For lifetime, multiply AOV and each cost line by the cohort-derived lifetime order count (here 1.98): revenue went from $238 to $469 and lifetime contribution margin to $197.

If no additional marketing was spent to drive repeat orders (customers returned via email list/organic), hold CAC flat and divide lifetime CM by the same CAC: $197 / $97 = 2.02, or about $99 profit per customer.
Interpret the result: a business that is roughly break-even on order one but 2x on lifetime can be profitable on every order once repeat purchases arrive; the presenter called this strong health.
caveats: Holding CAC flat for repeat orders assumes no incremental remarketing cost; if you pay to re-acquire or retarget, load that cost in.
First-order contribution margin below your CAC is only acceptable when the cohort data shows meaningful repeat orders.
The numbers here are one illustrative case, not target benchmarks for every store.

cards.title: Why 50% Off Sitewide Destroys Black Friday Unit Economics
cards.summary: The mechanical reason a sitewide percentage discount loses money even when traffic and conversion spike.
cards.use_when: Planning Black Friday or any sitewide promo and choosing between percentage discount and a multi-unit offer.
steps: Model baseline first: in the source example, 1.75% conversion, $75 CAC, $135 AOV, $124 after refunds/returns, $21 product COGS, $19 fulfillment COGS, leaving $84 contribution margin and only $9 after CAC.

Then model 50% off: conversion typically jumps to 4-5% and CAC can fall to about $33, but most buyers take one unit, cutting gross order value to about $68 and net order value to roughly 55% of normal AOV when returns/refunds are not offered.
Critical point: product and fulfillment COGS stay essentially fixed. In the example CM fell to $29 against $33 CAC, so every customer lost money - the presenter said he has seen this many times.
Watch the volume illusion: orders may jump from 5,000 to 20,000 and revenue skyrockets while contribution margin after CAC goes negative.
Warning sign for your store: a business already at only $9 CM-after-CAC per order ($50,000 on 5,000 orders) cannot absorb a 50% price cut.
caveats: Discounting also gives back revenue you would have collected from customers who would have bought anyway.

The presenter's stated policy: make money on the first order at Black Friday, because Black Friday customers have notoriously poor retention and many buy only once. Subscription brands may rationally choose otherwise.
The specific conversion, CAC and COGS figures are one brand's example, not universal.

cards.title: BOGO / Two-for-One as a Black Friday Cash Machine
cards.summary: Replace sitewide percentage discounts with a two-for-one or gift-with-purchase to deliver perceived value without giving back revenue.
cards.use_when: Designing a seasonal promotion where you want the conversion lift of a deep discount but positive per-order profit.
steps: Recognize the psychological equivalence: two-for-one reads to the customer as twice the product for half the price, so you generally get a similar conversion-rate and CAC lift to 50% off.

Model the mechanics: at $135 AOV with no returns, product COGS doubles from $21 to $42, shipping rises only marginally since both units ship in one box, and merchant fees stay around $4 because revenue is similar to a normal order.
Result in the source example: contribution margin of $69 versus $29 on the 50%-off promo, and CM after a lowered CAC of about $33 came to $36 - more than the brand made on a normal non-promo order.
Compare at equal volume: at the same 20,000 orders, the two-for-one generated roughly twice the revenue of 50% off and on the order of three-quarters of a million dollars in the example.
Generalize to your product mix: if unit COGS is low, test buy-two-get-one-free or another gift-with-purchase structure rather than a straight percentage cut.
Run the numbers for your own COGS before committing; the presenter's recommendation is to model it, not to assume it.
caveats: Only works when marginal product cost is low relative to price; heavy or expensive-to-ship goods erode the advantage.
Shipping cost per unit is assumed to rise only marginally because units ship together - verify with your 3PL rate card.
The dollar figures are a single illustrative case, not promised results.

cards.title: The Core Unit Economics Stack: CAC, AOV, CM, LTV and Their Ratios
cards.summary: Definitions and relationships for the five metrics that determine whether an ecommerce business model can work.
cards.use_when: Setting up your ecommerce financial model or explaining unit economics to your team before scaling spend.
steps: Define CAC as the marketing investment to acquire a customer for the first time, AOV as average basket size per order, and contribution margin as what's left from an order after direct per-order costs (product plus fulfillment).
Distinguish contribution margin (one order) from customer lifetime value (profit across the series of orders a customer makes) - LTV is CM extended over the customer's lifetime order count.
Compute CM:CAC as the first-order test and LTV:CAC as the lifetime test; a $100 CAC against $100 CM per order across five orders yields $500 profit and an LTV:CAC of 5.
Set the goal stated by the presenter: every incremental customer should be more profitable than the last, which means margins rise as the business scales.
Treat deteriorating unit economics as a hard stop: at 10x size, worsening economics can drive profit to zero or negative.
caveats: Ratios here are defined from the source's modeling approach; adapt the cost buckets to what your P&L actually captures.
LTV:CAC of 1.0 is not acceptable by the presenter's standard because it leaves nothing to cover overhead.

cards.title: Two Valid Models: Break Even on Order One, or Lose Early and Earn Later
cards.summary: When it is safe to lose money on the first order and when you must be profitable on it.
cards.use_when: Deciding how aggressively to bid on acquisition for one-time-purchase versus repeat-purchase product lines.
steps: Route one: hold margins and break even or better on the first order - required for product categories where most customers buy once, such as many apparel items.

Route two: run a very high lifetime order count (the source cites customers buying 5, 10, 15 times) so a first-order loss is recovered on the tail; the presenter cautions this only works for highly consumable or repeat-purchase products.
For repeat-consumable categories, consider subscribe-and-save / subscription box pricing as an antidote to low lifetime order counts.
Set the guardrail stated in the source: aim to at minimum break even on the first order for most businesses; only deliberately exceed that when the cohort data proves repeat behavior.
For one-time-buy categories, be careful about running CM:CAC below 1 on the first order - the presenter explicitly warns against it there.
caveats: A CM:CAC below 1 is only defensible with demonstrated high repeat rates; the source calls running it otherwise a way to lose money on every customer.
The 5-15 lifetime order range is the source's characterization of certain consumable businesses, not a benchmark for yours.

cards.title: Ecom Gross Margin vs Contribution Margin: Two Different Buckets
cards.summary: Separating product-level costs from per-order fulfillment costs so you know which costs scale with each order and which vary by shipment.
cards.use_when: Building your P&L model or diagnosing why margin differs between orders and shipping destinations.
steps: Bucket one - product costs: manufacturing, import freight, duties and taxes, i.e. everything to get product to the fulfillment center and ready to ship. In the source example this was 27% of a $175 order, or $47.
Bucket one result is the ecom gross margin: revenue minus product costs ($175 - $47 = $128 in the example).
Bucket two - fulfillment costs: pick and pack, materials, 3PL charges and shipping. These vary order by order, with shipping usually the largest line.
Contribution margin = revenue minus both buckets; in the example $175 - $47 - $40 of fulfillment = $83, and CAC should be at or below that $83.
Use the split diagnostically: product costs should be stable and improve with scale/supply-chain fixes, while fulfillment costs need per-destination or per-weight scrutiny.
caveats: This naming convention (ecom gross margin) is the source's, and differs from standard GAAP gross margin presentation.
Fulfillment cost variability means blended averages can hide unprofitable shipping lanes.

cards.title: Healthy Unit Economics Benchmarks Across the Business Lifecycle
cards.summary: How CAC, AOV, contribution margin and lifetime orders typically move from idea stage to late stage in a strong business.
cards.use_when: Benchmarking your own unit economics against a stage-appropriate expectation before raising or deploying growth capital.
steps: Idea phase (vision only): the source's plan was $65 CAC, $165 AOV, 60% contribution margin, 3 lifetime orders, giving $99 CM per order, 1.5 CM:CAC and roughly 5x LTV:CAC.
Launch phase: low CAC from friends/family but AOV only about $89 due to discounts and 39% contribution margin, with 1 lifetime order - CM:CAC around 1.0 is acceptable here.

Early stage (early channel fit, e.g. Facebook ads plus organic Instagram): 2,500 orders, $68 CAC, $134 AOV, $49 CM, older cohorts showing 1.7 lifetime orders and $112 LTV; CM:CAC about 1.0 and LTV:CAC about 1.6.
Growth phase: CAC drops slightly with organic mix, AOV normalizes to $148, CM 51%, LTV $196; CM:CAC 1.4 and LTV:CAC approaching 4.

Late stage: 250,000 orders, blended CAC down to $48, AOV up to $162 through more products and bundling, CM up to 65% from larger production runs and a fixed supply chain, 3.1 lifetime orders; CM:CAC 2.1 and LTV:CAC 6.7.
Target stated by the presenter: CM:CAC better than 1 at every stage, and roughly 5x or better LTV:CAC for a late-stage business driven by repeat customers.
caveats: These are the presenter's illustrative benchmark trajectories, not measured industry medians.
Excellent businesses can show 3-5x CM:CAC on the first order alone; matching 1.0 is not the ceiling.
Discounted periods legitimately lower AOV and margin - read them against the same period, not peak months.

cards.title: Sub-Optimal Pattern: Rising CAC With Flat Contribution Margin
cards.summary: The failure mode where a business scales spend faster than it fixes economics, losing money on every customer.
cards.use_when: Reviewing whether an influx of funding should be spent on more acquisition or on fixing supply chain and retention first.
steps: Watch for CAC rising while AOV and contribution margin stay flat or drift down (the source example: 68 to 79 CAC, then 123, then 149, as ad spend increased).
Check lifetime orders in the same review: in the example they only rose to 1.2, then 1.5, then 1.8, so repeat behavior never covered the rising acquisition cost.
Compute the ratios: CM:CAC fell below 1 on the first order and LTV:CAC landed at 0.87 and then 1.0 - which the presenter says leaves no money to cover opex.
Diagnose the actual constraint before adding budget: the example attributed weak contribution margin to unoptimized supply chain, a mislocated distribution center and air freight.
Verdict stated in the source: this business should not be scaling until unit economics are fixed, even if it raised a large Series A/B.
caveats: An LTV:CAC of exactly 1.0 is not a passing grade by the presenter's standard.
Some businesses with strong repeat buyers can run CM:CAC below 1 on the first order; one-time-buy businesses cannot.

cards.title: Splitting COGS Into Product and Fulfillment Buckets for Promo Modeling
cards.summary: The two-bucket COGS structure used to compare promotions and normal trading side by side.
cards.use_when: Building a promo P&L for Black Friday, bundles or free shipping tests, or recalculating contribution margin per order.
steps: Product COGS bucket: manufacturing cost plus duties and taxes, packaging, and inbound freight to the fulfillment center - in the example $15 manufacturing plus $6 other = $21.
Fulfillment COGS bucket: shipping and packing ($12), warehouse storage and pick costs ($3), and merchant/payment processing fees ($4) = $19 in the example.

Net AOV should be reduced for returns and refunds before computing anything else; the source notes losing roughly 5-10% of gross revenue to returns/refunds in many verticals ($135 to $124 in the example).
Contribution margin = net AOV minus both buckets ($124 - $21 - $19 = $84), then subtract CAC to get CM-after-CAC ($84 - $75 = $9).
When modeling a promo, hold product COGS fixed and adjust only the lines that actually move (merchant fees on lower revenue, marginally higher shipping for extra units in the same box).
caveats: The 5-10% returns figure is described as typical for many verticals, not universal - use your own returns data.
Promo best practice of not offering refunds or returns is a modeling assumption you must decide on deliberately.

cards.title: Three-Statement Model as the Diagnostic for a Profitable-but-Cash-Poor Store
cards.summary: Why ecommerce stores show positive net income and falling cash, and which statement lines to inspect in order.
cards.use_when: Investigating why your store's bank balance declines in months when the P&L shows profit.
steps: Orient with three lines side by side first: revenue (~$415K/month in the example), net income (positive every month), and free cash flow (negative $22K, then varying wildly - only two of six months had both net income and FCF positive).
Then walk the income statement for structural mismatches: product cost is not matched to when you buy inventory, only when you sell it.
Check depreciation versus real asset spend - depreciation is a smoothed, non-cash charge that hides lumpy purchase timing.
Check debt: interest shows on the P&L but loan principal repayments only appear on the balance sheet, so debt activity is invisible in net income.
Check taxes: the P&L may accrue monthly while actual quarterly estimated payments leave in lumps.
Then read the balance sheet for inventory changes (increase = cash out), accounts receivable, and capitalized software, before reconciling to the cash flow statement.
caveats: Positive net income is described as often misleading for startups; free cash flow clarifies what is really happening.
Some months with negative net income can increase cash - the source shows this pattern, so never infer cash direction from the P&L alone.

cards.title: Balance Sheet Cash Traps: Inventory, Capitalized Software, Quarterly Taxes
cards.summary: The three balance-sheet movements that most often explain cash going out while the P&L looks healthy.
cards.use_when: Planning a buying season, an engineering spend, or a tax payment quarter and forecasting whether cash can support it.
steps: Inventory: buying product is a lumpy cash outflow parked on the balance sheet. In the example, inventory rose $113K in one month (335 to 448) and this was the main driver of a $95K negative FCF on $77K net income; when inventory draws down, cash converts back in.

Capitalized software: payroll on engineers is moved off the P&L onto the balance sheet and amortized (typically 36 months for software). The example spent $240K over six months on the platform while only $40K hit the P&L.
Quarterly taxes: the P&L accrues monthly (e.g. $25K), but the balance sheet shows taxes building up and then leaving in lump payments (about $80K, then about $100K to the government).
Line of credit: reading the balance sheet showed roughly $25K/month of principal being paid down - cash leaving that never appears in net income.
Practical forecasting rule: before committing to an inventory buy, an engineering hire or a big marketing push, forecast the cash out date, not just the expense recognition date.
caveats: Capitalization rules and useful-life assumptions vary; confirm with your accountant rather than defaulting to 36 months.
This case is a constructed teaching model, so the dollar amounts are illustrative.

cards.title: Reading the Cash Flow Statement: Operating, Investing, Financing
cards.summary: How each section of the cash flow statement maps to ecommerce activity so you can trace where cash actually moves.
cards.use_when: Reviewing monthly cash movements and classifying spend the way a lender or investor will read it.
steps: Operating section starts with net income from the P&L, then adjusts: accounts receivable up = cash negative (customers owe you); accounts payable up = cash positive (you still owe suppliers); depreciation is stripped back out as non-cash; inventory change is booked from the balance sheet movement.
Investing section holds long-term asset purchases - buying assets, investing in the software platform, buying shares in another company. Salary paid one month is an expense, not an investment.
Financing section holds anything about capital structure: owner distributions, loans taken or repaid, outside capital in. Not day-to-day operations.
Free cash flow = operating cash flow minus investing cash flow; it is the money left after internal operations are fully funded, with no further obligations other than financing.
Use FCF as the decision number for what you can do next: pay down debt, take a distribution, or fund the next inventory buy.
caveats: The definition given is operating cash flow minus investing cash flow - some practitioners compute it other ways; be explicit about which you use.
In the example, one month showed net income of only $140 while cash flow was $272, so never substitute one for the other.

cards.title: Diagnosing Gross Margin Drops During Promo Months
cards.summary: Tracking gross margin percentage month over month to catch discount-driven margin erosion separate from volume effects.
cards.use_when: Reviewing monthly performance after a sale event to see whether volume gains were bought with margin.
steps: Track gross margin as a percentage of revenue, not just dollars, alongside order counts.
In the example, orders scaled from 3,000 to about 5,000, and in the month where orders more than doubled the gross margin percentage fell - the source attributes this directly to running a discount.

Cross-check the discount story against the COGS breakdown lines (product cost, import duty and inbound freight, pick and pack, shipping, merchant fees) to confirm the drop is price-driven rather than cost-driven.
Confirm recovery: the example then shows gross margin recovering in following months as discounting stops.
Use this pattern to set expectations before a promo: decide in advance what margin dilution you accept for the volume, and measure the actual against it the following month.
caveats: The source does not give a specific acceptable margin-dilution threshold; set your own based on contribution margin after CAC.
A margin drop coinciding with a supply-chain cost increase (air freight, for instance) will look similar - check COGS lines individually.
